newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS-Markets give mixed reaction to new NZ govt.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Markets give mixed reaction to new NZ govt.

text.p: The New Zealand dollar was sold sharply on Wednesday morning but the debt and share markets rallied hard on news that New Zealand First had joined with the ruling conservative National Party to form a new government.
Credit rating agency Moody's Investors Service gave its seal of approval, saying the new government would not materially affect New Zealand's credit rating.
The market's main worry is the appointment of NZ First leader Winston Peters as Treasurer. He is perceived as an interventionist with anti-foreign investor views.

The New Zealand dollar at 10 a.m. (2100 GMT) was nearly one U.S. cent lower than before the government announcement at US$0.6980/87, while short-term interest rates rallied 40 basis points and the share market opened 1.1 percent higher.

"The (forex) market initially responded to the blue (conservative) flag being waved, but then a sense of reality struck home that Winston Peters was the Treasurer," said National Bank chief foreign exchange dealer Stu Nattrass.

"The markets are struggling with the credibility of Peters as Treasurer given his views on foreign investment and the relative value of the exchange rate and the level of expenditure he desires. It's very difficult to see interest rates charging on," he said.

Bankers Trust Executive Vice President John Macfarlane said financial markets were relieved that changes to the Reserve Bank of NZ's operating framework were within the realm of what the market had expected and deemed reasonable.
This had been reinforced by RBNZ Governor Don Brash saying he was happy to work with the changes.
The bank's inflation target has been relaxed to 0-3 percent from 0-2 percent and sustainable growth has been spelt out as one of its targets.
Moody's Vice President, senior analyst Yves Lemay, told Reuters New Zealand's rating profile remained "firmly in the AA-1 rating category for its foreign currency debt and AAA for its domestic debt".
"The bottom line from our perspective is we don't anticipate new players in a new government would have any material impact on the rating," he said.
He said that despite budget surpluses lower than previously projected, New Zealand's budget position was the envy of most countries'.
Moody's also approved moves to defer 1997 planned tax cuts for a year and postpone plans to introduce compulsory pensions. These will be subject to a referendum.
Lemay said the relaxed inflation band had to be put into the overall context of macro-economic policy.
"So as long as the monetary policy continues to to focus on fighting inflation pressures, from our perspective that's a key element," he said.
"The currency is down, interest rates are down but there are lingering concerns about Peters as Treasurer," said Ord Minnett Equities Director John Rattray.
Rattray said the share market had been discounting for a Labour New Zealand First government so the announcement of a National-NZ First government was seen as a positive.
Bankers Trust New Zealand chief foreign exchange dealer Sean Brown said the New Zealand dollar was still an attractive currency compared with other less high yielding currencies.
"Our interest rates look extremely attractive compared with a lot of other places, especially given our sound economic fundamentals, so in the medium-term you look for a level to buy.
"In the short-term, the market is focused on the presence of Peters as Treasurer and what other changes we may get which make people nervous because they think the changes will be negative."
-- Wellington newsroom 64 4 4734 746
